claims.statement: For large uniform arrays, TOON serializes to 30-60% fewer input tokens than JSON at comparable retrieval accuracy.
claims.guidance: Use TOON for the big uniform/tabular payloads you feed INTO the model (tool results, row sets, retrieved records). Keep JSON where data is deeply nested or irregular.
claims.scope: Input side only, and only for uniform arrays. Nested or irregular objects show much smaller or negative gains, and on short payloads the 'prompt tax' of explaining the format to the model can erase the saving entirely. Says nothing about generation — see constrained-decoding-for-structured-output.

evidence.title: toon-format/toon — reference implementation, spec and benchmarks
Notation Matters: A Benchmark Study of Token-Optimized Formats in Agentic AI Systems
New Token-Oriented Object Notation (TOON) Hopes to Cut LLM Costs by Reducing Token Consumption
Token-Oriented Object Notation vs JSON: A Benchmark of Plain and Constrained Decoding Generation
evidence.note: Finds the advantage is often reduced by instructional overhead in shorter contexts.

claims.statement: JSON is the natural default for all agent I/O; serialization format is not a meaningful optimization lever.

evidence.title: Notation Matters: A Benchmark Study of Token-Optimized Formats in Agentic AI Systems

claims.supersession_reason: Format choice measurably moves cost: uniform arrays serialize 30-60% smaller in TOON at comparable retrieval accuracy, which makes serialization a real optimization lever on the input side rather than an aesthetic preference.

claims.statement: For structured model OUTPUT, constrained decoding gives the lowest token usage and plain JSON generation the best accuracy — token-optimized notations do not win here.
claims.guidance: Split the decision by direction. Use a token-optimized notation for what you feed in; use constrained decoding (or plain JSON) for what you ask the model to emit.
claims.scope: Benchmarked on one-shot in-context generation. Constrained decoding requires a serving stack that supports it — without one, plain JSON generation is the accuracy-preserving fallback.

evidence.title: Token-Oriented Object Notation vs JSON: A Benchmark of Plain and Constrained Decoding Generation

claims.statement: Because TOON is more token-efficient than JSON, asking the model to GENERATE TOON is also better than asking it to generate JSON.

evidence.title: Token-Oriented Object Notation vs JSON: A Benchmark of Plain and Constrained Decoding Generation

claims.supersession_reason: Benchmarked head-to-head, plain JSON generation had the best one-shot and final accuracy while constrained decoding used the fewest tokens; TOON was outperformed by constrained decoding even on simple structures. The input-side token saving does not transfer to the output side.

claims.statement: A newer SOTA model can be WORSE at your harness's custom tool schema than its older siblings, because it was RL-trained on a different harness's tools.
claims.guidance: Match your harness's tool schemas to what the target model was trained on — Claude on str-replace-style edits, OpenAI on apply_patch — and offer a model-matched edit tool in multi-model harnesses. Re-run tool-calling evals on every model upgrade.
claims.scope: Observed on custom edit-tool schemas in third-party harnesses. First-party harnesses whose tools the model was trained on do not show the regression.

evidence.title: Better Models, Worse Tools: SOTA models regress on non-native tool schemas

claims.statement: Swapping in the newest frontier model is a strict improvement for an existing harness.

evidence.title: Better Models, Worse Tools: SOTA models regress on non-native tool schemas

claims.supersession_reason: Measured on a third-party harness's custom edit tool, newer Claude models invented made-up fields that their older siblings got right. Model upgrades can regress harness-specific tool calling, so an upgrade is a change to re-evaluate, not a free win.

claims.statement: Coding-agent harnesses work better with few distinct tools and a lean system prompt of reasoning rather than rules.
claims.guidance: Keep the tool count small and the tools clearly distinct; write the system prompt as reasoning rather than rule lists; grow your eval suite out of real incidents; gate dangerous actions with a context-aware permission classifier rather than a static allowlist.
claims.scope: Described from first-party practice on one coding agent, not a controlled comparison — treat as a strong prior, not a measured result.

evidence.title: How the Claude Code team designs its harness

claims.statement: Headline benchmark F1 hides what actually matters for security scanning: groundedness, precision, and run-to-run stability.
claims.guidance: Score scanners on groundedness and run-to-run stability as first-class metrics, and evaluate precision on repos like yours — a matching F1 can still hide a precision gap that shifts cost onto human triage. Do not expect stacking models to fix a groundedness problem.

evidence.title: Auditing a cyber benchmark for groundedness: models reason, but 70% of real IDORs are missed
Kimi K3 code-security eval: matching F1 hides a precision gap

claims.statement: Prompt injection cannot be fully solved by context-based filtering: for any blocked flow an adversary can construct a context in which it appears legitimate.
claims.guidance: Design for containment rather than prevention: least-privilege tool scopes, human approval on irreversible actions, provenance tracking of untrusted context, and blast-radius limits that hold even when the model is fooled.
claims.scope: An impossibility argument about context-inferred legitimacy, not a claim that defenses are worthless — layered defenses still raise cost and catch known patterns.

evidence.title: AI Agents May Always Fall for Prompt Injections
Assessing Automated Prompt Injection Attacks in Agentic Environments
evidence.note: Large-scale red teaming: vulnerability to indirect injection persists across model families.

evidence.title: Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic Coding Assistants: A Systematic Analysis
evidence.note: Meta-analysis of 78 studies; taxonomy includes context-window manipulation as a delivery vector.

claims.statement: Prompt injection is fundamentally a filtering problem — a good input classifier plus an instruction-hierarchy system prompt solves it.

evidence.title: AI Agents May Always Fall for Prompt Injections
Assessing Automated Prompt Injection Attacks in Agentic Environments

claims.supersession_reason: Impossibility result: an adversary can always construct a context under which a blocked flow looks legitimate, and a defender who tightens norms to stop it starts blocking genuinely legitimate flows. Large-scale red teaming confirmed the vulnerability persists across model families, so filtering is a cost-raiser, not a solution.

claims.statement: Provenance-aware decision auditing — tracking how untrusted context propagates into an agent's decisions — is an effective defense against context-aware prompt injection.
claims.guidance: Worth piloting as a layer, but do not treat it as a boundary: keep least-privilege scopes and approval gates behind it.
claims.scope: Open question. The defense is demonstrated on specific benchmarks; the impossibility argument says no context-based defense can be complete. Both can be true — the unresolved part is how much residual risk remains in practice.

evidence.title: ARGUS: Defending LLM Agents Against Context-Aware Prompt Injection
evidence.note: Builds an influence provenance graph to track untrusted context into agent decisions.

evidence.title: AI Agents May Always Fall for Prompt Injections
evidence.note: Argues no context-based defense can be complete.

claims.statement: Poisoned preferences and instructions persist in agent long-term memory across sessions and resist normal in-conversation correction.
claims.guidance: Validate what is allowed to ENTER memory rather than trying to argue it out later. Treat an agent's memory and config files as protected assets with their own access control, change review, and backups.

evidence.title: Insecure coding preferences persist in LLM long-term memory and resist normal correction
Self-state attacks: corrupting an agent's own memory and config uses legitimate syscalls
What If Prompt Injection Never Left? Cross-Session Stored Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems

claims.statement: Commercial provider safety guardrails can refuse to assist during a real security incident, at exactly the moment you need the model most.
claims.guidance: Pre-stage a local open-weight forensic model so breach response does not depend on a provider's refusal behavior, and test that path before you need it.
claims.scope: Observed during a live agentic intrusion response. This is about availability of assistance under refusal, not about whether guardrails reduce harm overall.

evidence.title: Provider safety guardrails blocked incident response during the Hugging Face agentic intrusion

claims.statement: Prefer non-executable model formats and sandbox deserialization of any third-party model — a clean scanner result is weak evidence of safety.
claims.guidance: Load third-party weights only in a sandbox, prefer safetensors-style non-executable formats, and treat scanner output as one signal rather than an admission gate.

evidence.title: ShadowPickle: pickle-VM import tricks evade ten model scanners and four model hubs

claims.statement: A clean model-scanner result is adequate evidence that a third-party model artifact is safe to load.

evidence.title: ShadowPickle: pickle-VM import tricks evade ten model scanners and four model hubs

claims.supersession_reason: Pickle-VM import tricks evaded ten separate model scanners and four model hubs. A clean scan result no longer distinguishes a safe artifact from an evasive one, so scanning cannot be the admission gate.

claims.statement: Agent-generated PRs need automated secret and dependency-integrity gates — human review demonstrably does not catch that class of issue.
claims.guidance: Put automated secret scanning and dependency-integrity checks in the required-checks set for agent PRs, and keep human review for design and logic where it actually performs.
claims.scope: Measured on agent-generated PRs; 38.9% carried a security smell, though humans still introduce most of the severe defects overall.

evidence.title: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs carry a security smell — but humans introduce most of the real ones

claims.statement: Normal human code review is sufficient to catch the security problems in agent-generated pull requests.

evidence.title: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs carry a security smell

claims.supersession_reason: Measured across agent-generated PRs, 38.9% carried a security smell and human review demonstrably did not catch the secret and dependency-integrity class. Review remains valuable for logic and design, but it is not the control for this risk.

claims.statement: npm supply-chain payloads delivered at IMPORT time defeat --ignore-scripts, and a valid provenance attestation does not indicate the package is trustworthy.
claims.guidance: Do not treat --ignore-scripts or provenance attestation as the control. Pin and review dependency updates, run untrusted first-import in a sandbox, and monitor runtime egress from build and test jobs.

evidence.title: Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply-chain compromise: import-time payload delivery

claims.statement: Installing with --ignore-scripts, plus checking for a provenance attestation, is adequate protection against npm supply-chain compromise.

evidence.title: Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply-chain compromise: import-time payload delivery

claims.supersession_reason: The AsyncAPI compromise delivered its payload at import time, which --ignore-scripts does not prevent, and it shipped with a valid provenance attestation. Both controls target the wrong stage of the lifecycle.

claims.statement: LLM applications that mix trusted instructions with untrusted input are permanently vulnerable to instruction hijacking; the surface cannot be closed by prompt engineering alone.

evidence.title: The Dual LLM pattern
Not what you've signed up for: Compromising real-world LLM-integrated applications with indirect prompt injection

claims.guidance: Design agentic systems assuming injection succeeds sometimes: least-privilege tool scopes, human approval on irreversible actions, blast-radius caps that hold even when the model is fooled.

claims.statement: Indirect prompt injection — hostile instructions embedded in documents, web pages, or tool outputs that the LLM reads at run time — is a demonstrated attack vector against real production LLM assistants.

evidence.title: Not what you've signed up for
Hacking GitHub Copilot Chat via indirect prompt injection

claims.guidance: Treat every retrieval-augmented context as untrusted input. Never let retrieved content unilaterally cause a tool call with side effects.

claims.statement: Adversarial suffixes crafted against one aligned model transfer with non-trivial success to other models of similar family, including closed-source ones.

evidence.title: Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models

claims.guidance: Alignment training on one model is not evidence of alignment for another. Run adversarial evals against your deployed model, not a proxy.

claims.statement: Splitting agent architecture into a privileged planner LLM that never sees untrusted input, and a quarantined LLM that processes untrusted input but has no tool access, contains prompt injection to non-privileged operations.

evidence.title: The Dual LLM pattern

claims.guidance: For high-authority agents, use a two-tier architecture: the planner sees only tool schemas + user intent; the reader/quarantined LLM sees untrusted content and returns structured summaries the planner cannot execute as commands.

claims.statement: Constitutional AI-style training (self-critique + revision against a written set of principles) reduces the fragility of hand-tuned refusal training and gives the training process an inspectable specification.

evidence.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback

claims.guidance: Prefer alignment techniques with a written, auditable spec over hand-tuned refusal datasets you can't inspect.

claims.statement: Loading a pickle-based model file (PyTorch .pt/.bin) is equivalent to running arbitrary code; the format has no sandbox and no way to introspect what will execute at load time short of manual reversing.

evidence.title: Never a dill moment
Pickle scanning

claims.guidance: Prefer safetensors for any model you didn't personally train. If you must load pickles, do it in a container with no outbound network.

claims.statement: Adversaries publish typosquatted model repositories on public hubs (name variants of popular models) that ship with malicious pickle payloads or exfiltration hooks; several have been observed in the wild on Hugging Face.

evidence.title: Malicious ML models with silent backdoor found on Hugging Face

claims.guidance: Pin model artifacts by revision hash, not by name. Verify the model card against the vendor's known channels.

claims.statement: MCP tool descriptions are consumed by the model as part of the system prompt; a hostile MCP server can inject instructions via tool metadata alone, without needing the tool to be called.

evidence.title: MCP Security Notification: Tool Poisoning Attacks

claims.guidance: Version-pin and change-review every MCP tool description. Treat metadata updates as system-prompt changes requiring re-approval.

claims.statement: An agent's tool selection can be influenced by content in its context window; adversarial content in retrieved documents can cause the agent to prefer a hostile tool over the intended one.

evidence.title: Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic Systems

claims.guidance: Do not present tools whose selection can be influenced by untrusted context unless the tool is safe when called on adversarial input.

claims.statement: Once an LLM assistant persists user-provided information to a long-term memory store, adversarial content can be planted in one session and reliably retrieved into a future session, producing effects that outlast the poisoning conversation.

evidence.title: ChatGPT: Hacking Memories with Prompt Injection

claims.guidance: Gate what enters long-term memory with a policy check, not a post-hoc filter. Treat memory writes as security-relevant.

claims.statement: Public benchmark datasets used to evaluate LLM security leak into the training corpora of later models, inflating scores without corresponding capability change.

evidence.title: Data Contamination Quiz

claims.guidance: Rotate held-out red-team prompts; treat any published adversarial dataset as compromised for future models.

claims.statement: SSRF guards on user-input URLs are not sufficient for agent applications: the agent can be steered into making outbound calls from tool responses, retrieval results, or MCP metadata.

evidence.title: SSRF (OWASP)

claims.guidance: Apply the private-IP dialer guard to every outbound HTTP client in an agent runtime — not just the user-facing one. Re-validate on redirect.

claims.statement: Any code that opens a file whose path derives from user input must canonicalize the resolved target and verify it stays within the intended sandbox; validating the raw path string is insufficient.

evidence.title: CWE-22

claims.guidance: Use realpath() then verify prefix. Never trust the input string alone.

claims.statement: Installing a package with pip, npm, or gem executes arbitrary code at install time by default. Treat 'installed a dep' as 'ran their code'.

evidence.title: Supply chain best practices

claims.guidance: Do first-touch installs in a sandbox. Where possible, prefer --ignore-scripts + explicit build orchestration.

claims.statement: Typosquatted packages are regularly uploaded to public registries with malicious install-time payloads; the technique remains effective because dependency selection is often typed manually.

evidence.title: Typosquatting on npm

claims.guidance: Prefer install from lockfile only; audit any hand-added dependency's provenance.

claims.statement: AWS IMDSv1 is trivially exploitable from any code that can cause an HTTP GET to 169.254.169.254; agent workloads that may fetch user-provided URLs must disable v1 in favor of v2.

evidence.title: Get the full benefits of IMDSv2

claims.guidance: Set HttpTokens=required on all EC2 instances hosting agent runtimes.

claims.statement: Long-lived static cloud credentials in CI or on developer machines are the highest-frequency root cause of breach in cloud environments; short-lived OIDC / role-assumption flows should be used for every automated workload.

evidence.title: Workload identity federation

claims.guidance: Migrate CI to OIDC federation. Enforce a max credential age on IAM users.

claims.statement: LLMs generate import statements for packages that do not exist ('slopsquatting'); attackers observe these hallucinated names and register malicious packages to catch the next developer who copies the generated code.

evidence.title: We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations

claims.guidance: Every LLM-suggested dependency must be verified against the actual registry before pinning.

claims.statement: Signature-based detection under-performs against LLM-authored malware because trivial regeneration produces novel binaries at zero cost, while behavior and delivery-chain signals remain stable.

evidence.title: Using LLMs to obfuscate malicious JavaScript

claims.guidance: Weight EDR and behavioral analytics over hash-based feeds for AI-authored threat classes.

claims.statement: Mobile applications that render web content in a WebView with JS bridges exposed to native code create a persistent cross-context attack surface — any XSS in the rendered content becomes device-level RCE.

evidence.title: Insecure WebView native bridge

claims.guidance: Never expose native bridges to WebViews that render third-party content.

claims.statement: Adding more tools to an agent's available set beyond a modest number (roughly 10–20) degrades tool-selection accuracy and task success, even when the added tools are individually well-scoped.

evidence.title: ToolLLM

claims.guidance: Curate the tool set. Retire tools whose calls the eval suite shows agents get wrong more than they get right.

claims.statement: Chain-of-thought accuracy gains measured on single-turn benchmarks do not reliably transfer to multi-turn agent tasks where the model must revise its plan across steps.

evidence.title: Chain-of-thought reasoning without prompting

claims.guidance: Evaluate agents on the multi-turn task, not a single-turn proxy.

claims.statement: In production RAG systems, retrieval quality dominates generation quality as a determinant of end-task accuracy; larger models cannot compensate for a bad retriever.

evidence.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLMs: A Survey

claims.guidance: Invest in retrieval evals (recall@k, reranker quality) before spending on bigger generator models.

claims.statement: Hybrid search (BM25 + dense vectors) outperforms pure vector retrieval on most enterprise/technical corpora, because vector embeddings underweight exact term matches that carry high signal.

evidence.title: Hybrid Search Explained

claims.guidance: Default to hybrid retrieval unless you've measured that pure-vector wins on your specific corpus.

claims.statement: Long-context models do not eliminate the need for retrieval: they exhibit lost-in-the-middle effects, cost grows linearly with context size, and per-token attention drops on distant tokens.

evidence.title: Lost in the Middle

claims.guidance: Retrieval + a short, relevant context still beats stuffing a long context on cost, latency, and accuracy for most tasks.

claims.statement: LLM-as-judge evaluators exhibit systematic bias toward longer, more elaborate answers, independent of quality; the bias survives common mitigations.

evidence.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena

claims.guidance: Cross-check LLM-judge scores with pairwise human eval on a small sample.

claims.statement: SWE-bench scores do not linearly predict agent performance on production engineering tasks; the benchmark rewards a specific style of small-diff bug-fix.

evidence.title: SWE-bench

claims.guidance: Treat SWE-bench as one data point, not a complete picture. Build in-house evals on your task mix.

claims.statement: Production system prompts are load-bearing configuration and should be version-controlled, code-reviewed, and evaluated on regression suites.

evidence.title: Prompt injection and the security of AI applications

claims.guidance: Store prompts in the same repo as the code that calls them. Run eval on every prompt change and every model change.

claims.statement: Few-shot prompting accuracy is highly sensitive to example ordering, whitespace, and demarcation choices, in ways that look like model regressions if not controlled for.

evidence.title: Calibrate Before Use

claims.guidance: Freeze prompt formatting when evaluating model changes.

claims.statement: A model's actual capability ceiling is typically higher than what standard prompting elicits; targeted prompting or scaffolding can unlock capabilities the base eval missed.

evidence.title: Responsible Scaling Policy

claims.guidance: Do not build a safety case on 'the model can't do X' from a base-eval measurement alone.

claims.statement: 8-bit and 4-bit quantization of open-weights models preserves most benchmark accuracy (within 1–3 points) while cutting memory footprint proportionally.

evidence.title: SpQR

claims.guidance: Default to quantized weights for local inference of models ≥7B on consumer hardware.

claims.statement: Coding assistants generate calls to functions and APIs that do not exist in the target library or version — plausible spelling, correct-looking signature, no runtime existence.

evidence.title: Hallucinations in Code Generation

claims.guidance: Any LLM-suggested import or API call must be validated against the actual library documentation for the pinned version.

claims.statement: Reviewing an LLM's proposed change as a diff catches more defects than reviewing the resulting full file.

evidence.title: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity

claims.guidance: Prefer tools that present LLM changes as diffs. Reviewer must sign off on the specific lines that changed.
